title: Rank of a matrix by Echelon form

sections.heading: 2.7 (1) Rank of a Matrix
paragraphs: If we select any r rows and r columns from any matrix A, deleting all the other rows and columns, then the determinant formed by these r × r elements is called the minor of A of order r. Clearly, there will be a number of different minors of the same order, got by deleting different rows and columns from the same matrix.
Def. A matrix is said to be of rank r when
bullets: (i) it has at least one non-zero minor of order r, and
(ii) every minor of order higher than r vanishes.
Briefly, the rank of a matrix is the largest order of any non-vanishing minor of the matrix.
The rank of a matrix A shall be denoted by \(\rho(A)\).

sections.heading: Observations
bullets: Obs. 1. Rank of A and its transpose is the same i.e. \(\rho(A)=\rho(A\prime)\).
Obs. 2. Rank of a null matrix is zero.
Obs. 3. Rank of a non-singular square matrix of order r is r.
Obs. 4. If a matrix has a non-zero minor of order r, its rank is \(\ge r\). If all minors of a matrix of order \(r+1\) are zero, its rank is \(\le r\).

sections.heading: 2.7 (2) Elementary transformation of a matrix
paragraphs: The following operations, three of which refer to rows and three to columns are known as elementary transformations:
bullets: I. The interchange of any two rows (columns).
II. The multiplication of any row (column) by a non-zero number.
III. The addition of a constant multiple of the elements of any row (column) to the corresponding elements of any other row (column).

Notation. The elementary row transformations will be denoted by the following symbols: (i) \(R_{ij}\) for the interchange of the ith and jth rows. (ii) \(kR_i\) for multiplication of the ith row by k. (iii) \(R_i+pR_j\) for addition to the ith row, p times the jth row.
The corresponding column transformation will be denoted by writing C in place of R.

Elementary transformations do not change either the order or rank of a matrix. While the value of the minors may get changed by the transformation I and II, their zero or non-zero character remains unaffected.

intro: Gauss–Seidel is an iterative method for solving simultaneous linear equations. Instead of obtaining the solution through one finite elimination process, we begin with approximate values and repeatedly improve them. The unknowns are calculated one after another, and each newly calculated value is used immediately in the next calculation. This immediate use of newly calculated values is the key difference from Jacobi iteration.

explainers.summary: What “stretched” and “shrunk” really mean — and why direction matters
explainers.title: Think of an eigenvector as an arrow whose direction survives the matrix transformation
paragraphs: Think of a vector as an arrow starting at the origin. For example, \(X=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}\) is an arrow from \((0,0)\) to \((2,1)\).

If we multiply this vector by 3, then \(3X=\begin{bmatrix}6\\3\end{bmatrix}\). The endpoint moves farther away, but the arrow still points along the same line. Both coordinates became 3 times larger, so the vector is 3 times longer. This is what we mean by stretching a vector.
Similarly, \(\dfrac12X=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0.5\end{bmatrix}\) still points in the same direction, but is only half as long. This is what we mean by shrinking a vector.
bullets: \(\lambda>1\): the vector is stretched.
\(0<\lambda<1\): the vector is shrunk.
A negative \(\lambda\) keeps the vector on the same line but reverses its direction. For example, \(\lambda=-2\) makes it twice as long and points it the opposite way.

sections.heading: A matrix is a transformation machine
paragraphs: A matrix takes a vector and transforms it. For most vectors, this changes both the vector's length and its direction.

For example, take \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\). If \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\), then \(AX=\begin{bmatrix}2\\0\end{bmatrix}=2X\). The arrow stays on the x-axis and only becomes twice as long, so \(X\) is an eigenvector and \(\lambda=2\).

Likewise, if \(X=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\), then \(AX=\begin{bmatrix}0\\3\end{bmatrix}=3X\). The direction is unchanged and the vector becomes 3 times longer, so this is also an eigenvector, with \(\lambda=3\).

sections.heading: What happens to an ordinary vector?
paragraphs: With the same matrix, take \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(AX=\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}\).

There is no single number \(\lambda\) for which \(\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}=\lambda\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\). If we multiplied \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) by 2 we would get \(\begin{bmatrix}2\\2\end{bmatrix}\), and by 3 we would get \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\3\end{bmatrix}\), not \(\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\end{bmatrix}\). So the arrow has turned, and \(\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) is not an eigenvector.

sections.heading: Priyanka's example
paragraphs: Geometrically, the arrow originally goes from \((0,0)\) to \((4,1)\), and after the matrix acts it goes from \((0,0)\) to \((24,6)\). Since \((24,6)=6(4,1)\), it is still pointing along exactly the same line; it is simply 6 times longer. Therefore \(X=\begin{bmatrix}4\\1\end{bmatrix}\) is an eigenvector and \(\lambda=6\) is its eigenvalue.

sections.heading: Why does the formula become \((A-\lambda I)X=0\)?
paragraphs: Start with the defining equation \(AX=\lambda X\). Bring everything to one side: \(AX-\lambda X=0\).
Because \(IX=X\), we can write \(\lambda X=\lambda IX\). Hence \(AX-\lambda IX=0\), and taking \(X\) common gives \[\boxed{(A-\lambda I)X=0}.\]

We want a non-zero eigenvector \(X\). For this homogeneous system to have a non-zero solution, the coefficient matrix \(A-\lambda I\) must be singular. Therefore its determinant must be zero: \[\boxed{|A-\lambda I|=0}.\] This is the characteristic equation; solving it gives the eigenvalues.

sections.heading: Main idea to remember
paragraphs: \[\boxed{\text{Eigenvector = a direction that the matrix does not turn}}\]
\[\boxed{\text{Eigenvalue = the scale factor for that direction}}\]

For Priyanka's example, \[\boxed{\begin{bmatrix}5&4\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\1\end{bmatrix}=6\begin{bmatrix}4\\1\end{bmatrix}}.\] The direction \((4,1)\) stays the same and is stretched by a factor of 6.

sections.heading: 2.14 Properties of Eigen Values
bullets: I. A square matrix \(A\) and its transpose \(A^{T}\) have the same eigenvalues, since \(|A^{T}-\lambda I|=|(A-\lambda I)^{T}|=|A-\lambda I|\).
II. The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal elements. Hence the eigenvalues of a diagonal matrix are just its diagonal elements.
III. The eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are either 0 or 1. If \(A^2=A\) and \(AX=\lambda X\), then \(\lambda^2X=\lambda X\), so \(\lambda(\lambda-1)=0\).
IV. The sum of the eigenvalues of a matrix is its trace, i.e. the sum of the principal diagonal elements.
V. The product of the eigenvalues of a matrix \(A\) is equal to \(|A|\).
VI. If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of a non-singular matrix \(A\), then \(1/\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(A^{-1}\).
VII. If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix \(A\), then \(1/\lambda\) is also an eigenvalue of \(A\), because \(A^{-1}=A^{T}\) and \(A\) and \(A^{T}\) have the same eigenvalues.

VIII. If \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues of \(A\), then \(A^m\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_1^m,\lambda_2^m,\ldots,\lambda_n^m\) for a positive integer \(m\); the corresponding eigenvectors remain the same.

book_refs.note: Index, signature and classification of quadratic forms

paragraphs: Let \(Q=X^{T}AX\) be a quadratic form in \(n\) variables. The number of positive terms in its canonical form is called the index. The signature is the difference between the number of positive and negative terms in the canonical form.
bullets: If the rank of \(A\) is \(r\) and the index is \(s\), the form is positive definite if \(r=n\) and \(s=n\).
It is negative definite if \(r=n\) and \(s=0\).
It is positive semidefinite if \(r<n\) and \(s=r\).
It is negative semidefinite if \(r<n\) and \(s=0\).
It is indefinite in all other cases.

Equivalently: positive definite if all eigenvalues of \(A\) are positive; negative definite if all are negative; positive semidefinite if all are non-negative with at least one zero; negative semidefinite if all are non-positive with at least one zero; indefinite if some eigenvalues are positive and others negative.

sections.heading: Curve-tracing reference checklist
paragraphs: For an implicit Cartesian equation, inspect symmetry, the origin, tangents and asymptotes before drawing the curve.
bullets: Only even powers of y imply symmetry about the x-axis; only even powers of x imply symmetry about the y-axis.
If interchanging x and y leaves the equation unchanged, the curve is symmetric about y=x.
If there is no constant term, test the origin. The lowest-degree homogeneous terms give candidate tangents at the origin.
For an oblique asymptote write y=mx+c and compare the highest remaining powers, retaining all required coefficient equations.

sections.heading: Polar asymptote reference
paragraphs: For a polar curve expressed as \(1/r=f(\theta)\), the reference formula for an asymptote is \(r\sin(\theta-\alpha)=1/f\prime(\alpha)\), where \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f\prime(\alpha)\ne0\). This gives an asymptote candidate; it is not a complete polar-curve tracing procedure.

sections.heading: 5.1 Functions of two or more variables

book_refs.note: 5.1 Functions of two or more variables

paragraphs: An area \(A=xy\) depends on two lengths; a volume \(V=xyz\) depends on three. If each pair \((x,y)\) determines a definite value of \(z\), write \(z=f(x,y)\); \(x,y\) are independent variables and \(z\) is the dependent variable.
Points \((x,y)\) form a region in the xy-plane. A region containing its boundary is closed. A circular neighbourhood of \((a,b)\) has the form \((x-a)^2+(y-b)^2<\delta^2\).
The function tends to a limit \(l\) as \((x,y)\to(a,b)\) if \(f(x,y)\to l\) independently of the path of approach.
Precisely: for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f(x,y)-l|<\varepsilon\) whenever \(0<(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2<\delta^2\) within the domain.
Continuity at \((a,b)\) requires that the limit exists and equals \(f(a,b)\). Continuity in a region means continuity at every point of that region.
bullets: If \(f\to l\), \(g\to m\), then \(f+g\to l+m\), \(fg\to lm\), and \(f/g\to l/m\) when \(m\ne0\).
The corresponding sum, product and quotient continuity rules hold wherever their values are defined.

accordions.title: Illustration — path-dependent limit
paragraphs: Along \(y=mx\), \(m\ne-1\), the ratio is \((1-m)/(1+m)\), independent of the distance from the origin but dependent on the slope.
In particular, along \(y=0\) it is 1; along \(x=0\) it is −1. These disagree.
accordions.final_answer: The two-variable limit does not exist.

sections.heading: 5.11 Maxima and minima of two-variable functions

book_refs.note: 5.11 Maxima and minima of two-variable functions

paragraphs: A function has a local maximum at \((a,b)\) if nearby values are no greater than \(f(a,b)\); it has a local minimum if nearby values are no smaller. With strict inequalities away from the point the extremum is strict. The greatest or least value over an entire specified domain is a global extremum.
For a differentiable function at an interior extremum, the necessary stationary conditions are \(f_x(a,b)=f_y(a,b)=0\). A stationary point need not be an extremum.
Put \(r=f_{xx}(a,b),s=f_{xy}(a,b),t=f_{yy}(a,b)\) and \(D=rt-s^2\). The quadratic part of the change is \((rh^2+2shk+tk^2)/2\).
bullets: If \(D>0,r>0\): a local minimum.
If \(D>0,r<0\): a local maximum.
If \(D<0\): a saddle point; there are nearby values both above and below \(f(a,b)\).
If \(D=0\): the test is inconclusive. Examine higher-order terms or suitable paths.
First solve both stationary equations without losing zero-factor cases, then classify every resulting point or stationary set.

accordions.title: Example 5.46
paragraphs: \(f_x=4x^3-4x+4y\), \(f_y=4y^3+4x-4y\). The stationary equations sum to \(x^3+y^3=0\), so for real x,y, \(y=-x\).
Substitute into \(x^3-x+y=0\): \(x(x^2-2)=0\). The stationary points are \((0,0),(\sqrt2,-\sqrt2),(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\).
\(r=12x^2-4,s=4,t=12y^2-4\). At the two nonzero points, \(r=t=20\), \(D=rt-s^2=384>0\), and \(r>0\), so both are minima. Their function value is −8.
At zero, \(D=0\). Along \(y=0\), \(f=x^4-2x^2<0\) near zero, but along \(y=x\), \(f=2x^4>0\). Thus the origin is a saddle.
accordions.final_answer: Minima −8 at \((\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)\) and \((-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\); a saddle at \((0,0)\).

accordions.title: Example 5.47
question_paragraphs: Discuss the maxima and minima of \(f(x,y)=x^3y^2(1-x-y)\).
paragraphs: If \(xy\ne0\), solve \(4x+3y=3,\ 2x+3y=2\) to obtain \((x,y)=(1/2,1/3)\). Also every point on either coordinate axis is stationary; these cases must not be discarded when dividing by x or y.

On \(y=0\), the sign of nearby f is the sign of \(x^3(1-x-y)\), since \(y^2\ge0\). Thus \((x,0)\) is a non-strict local minimum of value zero for \(0<x<1\), and a non-strict local maximum of value zero for \(x<0\) or \(x>1\).

At \((1,0)\), the path x=1 gives \(f=-y^3\), so it is not an extremum. At every point on x=0, nearby values of both signs occur: for \(y\ne1\) vary the sign of x while keeping the coefficient \(1-x-y\) fixed in sign; at \((0,1)\) compare y=1 with y=1−2x. At the origin use y=x.
accordions.final_answer: A strict local maximum \(1/432\) occurs at \((1/2,1/3)\); the y=0 stationary line also has the non-strict extrema described above. Points on x=0 and \((1,0)\) are not extrema.

accordions.title: Example 5.48
question_paragraphs: Locate and classify the stationary points of \(f(x,y)=2(x-y)^2-x^4-y^4\).
paragraphs: \(f_x=4(x-y)-4x^3\), \(f_y=-4(x-y)-4y^3\). Adding the stationary equations gives \(x^3+y^3=0\), hence y=−x.
Substitution yields \(4x(2-x^2)=0\), so the points are \((0,0),(\sqrt2,-\sqrt2),(-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\).
\(r=4-12x^2,s=-4,t=4-12y^2\). At the nonzero points \(r=t=-20,D=384>0\); both are maxima with value 8.
At zero, \(D=0\). Along y=−x, \(f=8x^2-2x^4>0\) sufficiently near zero; along y=x, \(f=-2x^4<0\).
accordions.final_answer: Maxima 8 at \((\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)\), \((-\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\); the origin is a saddle.

accordions.title: Example 5.49
question_paragraphs: Prove that a rectangular solid of maximum volume inscribed in a sphere is a cube, and find its maximum volume.
paragraphs: Let d be the sphere’s diameter and x,y,z the positive full edge lengths. A body diagonal spans the diameter, so \(x^2+y^2+z^2=d^2\), and \(V=xyz\).
At an interior stationary point, subtraction gives \(x^2=y^2\). Then \(x^2=y^2=d^2/3\), and the constraint gives \(z^2=d^2/3\).
All edges are positive, so \(x=y=z=d/\sqrt3\). The volume vanishes on the boundary of the feasible positive region; the positive interior stationary value is the maximum.
accordions.final_answer: The solid is a cube of edge \(d/\sqrt3\), with \(V_{\max}=d^3/(3\sqrt3)\).

title: Maxima and minima of functions of three variables using method of Lagrange multipliers

sections.heading: 5.12 Lagrange’s method of undetermined multipliers
paragraphs: When variables are linked by constraints, eliminating a variable may be inconvenient. For a function \(u=f(x,y,z)\) subject to \(\phi(x,y,z)=0\), introduce
Solve \(F_x=F_y=F_z=0\) together with the constraint. For two independent regular constraints use two multipliers and include both constraints.

These equations identify candidate stationary values; they do not by themselves distinguish maxima from minima. Check feasibility, singular cases, boundaries where relevant, and the nature of each candidate.

accordions.title: Example 5.50
question_paragraphs: A rectangular box open at the top has volume 32 cubic feet. Find dimensions requiring the least material.
paragraphs: Let x,y be base edges and z the height. \(xyz=32\) and area \(S=xy+2yz+2zx=xy+64/x+64/y\).
At x=y=4, \(S_{xx}=2,S_{xy}=1,S_{yy}=2\), so \(D=3>0\) and \(S_{xx}>0\). The area grows toward the positive-domain boundary, so this is the required minimum.
Equivalently, set \(F=xy+2yz+2zx+\lambda(xyz-32)\). Its three derivative equations imply x=y=2z, and the constraint again gives 4,4,2.
accordions.final_answer: Base 4 ft × 4 ft, height 2 ft; minimum area 48 ft².

accordions.title: Example 5.51
question_paragraphs: (ii) Find the minimum of \(x^2+y^2+z^2\) subject to \(ax+by+cz=p\).

solution_parts.label: (i)
paragraphs: Use the positive-domain interpretation \(a,m,n,p>0\), \(x,y,z\ge0\). For an interior point, set \(F=x^my^nz^p+\lambda(x+y+z-a)\).

Thus \(x=am/(m+n+p)\), \(y=an/(m+n+p)\), \(z=ap/(m+n+p)\). The logarithm \(m\log x+n\log y+p\log z\) is strictly concave, so this interior stationary point is a maximum; the product is zero on the boundary.

solution_parts.label: (ii)
paragraphs: With \(A=a^2+b^2+c^2>0\), substituting into the constraint gives \(\lambda=-2p/A\). Therefore \((x,y,z)=p(a,b,c)/A\).
The value is \(p^2/A\). For any feasible vector write \((x,y,z)=p(a,b,c)/A+w\), where \((a,b,c)\cdot w=0\). Its squared length is \(p^2/A+\lVert w\rVert^2\), proving the minimum.

explainers.title: Domain for part (i)
paragraphs: The positive-domain interpretation a,m,n,p>0 and x,y,z≥0 is necessary for the stated weighted-product maximum. These restrictions are made explicit in the working; without them the unqualified maximum claim need not hold.

accordions.title: Example 5.52
question_paragraphs: Find the maximum and minimum distances of \((3,4,12)\) from the sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2=4\).
paragraphs: Optimise \(f=(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2+(z-12)^2\) subject to the radius-two sphere. For \(F=f+\lambda(x^2+y^2+z^2-4)\), differentiation gives \((1+\lambda)(x,y,z)=(3,4,12)\).
The constraint gives \(4=169/(1+\lambda)^2\), hence \(1+\lambda=\pm13/2\). The candidate points are \(\pm(6,8,24)/13\).

The external point has distance 13 from the origin. The nearest candidate is in its direction at radius 2, giving 13−2=11. The opposite candidate gives 13+2=15. Continuity on the compact sphere ensures that these candidates supply the extrema.
accordions.final_answer: Minimum distance 11; maximum distance 15 for the stated sphere.

accordions.title: Example 5.53
question_paragraphs: Show that the rectangular solid of maximum volume inscribed in a sphere is a cube.
paragraphs: Let 2x,2y,2z be its full positive edge lengths and R the sphere’s radius. \(V=8xyz\), with \(x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2\).
The stationary equations are \(8yz+2\lambda x=0\), \(8xz+2\lambda y=0\), \(8xy+2\lambda z=0\). Multiply by x,y,z respectively: the first terms are all 8xyz, so \(x^2=y^2=z^2\).
With positive edges \(x=y=z=R/\sqrt3\). Boundary volumes vanish, and the interior value is positive.
accordions.final_answer: A cube with edge \(2R/\sqrt3\); maximum volume \(8R^3/(3\sqrt3)\).

accordions.title: Example 5.54
question_paragraphs: A tent on a square base of side x has vertical sides of height y and a regular-pyramid top of height h. For fixed capacity, find x and y in terms of h that minimise the canvas area.
paragraphs: With no canvas floor, \(V=x^2y+x^2h/3\), and \(S=4xy+x\sqrt{x^2+4h^2}\). The slant height of each triangular roof panel is \(\sqrt{h^2+x^2/4}\).
Set \(F=S+\lambda(V-V_0)\). The y-equation gives \(4x+\lambda x^2=0\), hence \(\lambda=-4/x\).
The h-equation is \(4xh/\sqrt{x^2+4h^2}+\lambda x^2/3=0\). Substitution gives \(\sqrt{x^2+4h^2}=3h\), hence \(x=\sqrt5h\).
Put \(x^2=5h^2\), \(\lambda x=-4\), and the square root3h: \(4y+3h+5h/3-8y-8h/3=0\), so \(y=h/2\).

explainers.title: PankusDesk minimum check
paragraphs: Eliminate y using the fixed capacity V: \(S=4V/x-4xh/3+x\sqrt{x^2+4h^2}\). For each positive x, the h-dependent expression is convex and is minimised at \(h=x/\sqrt5\). Therefore \(S\ge4V/x+\sqrt5x^2/3\).

This last expression tends to infinity at both positive-domain ends. Its unique critical point is \(x^3=6V/\sqrt5\), where \(y=V/x^2-h/3=h/2>0\). Thus the stationary dimensions are feasible and attain the global lower bound.

accordions.title: Example 5.55
question_paragraphs: For \(u=a^3x^2+b^3y^2+c^3z^2\) with \(x^{-1}+y^{-1}+z^{-1}=1\), show the stationary values occur at \(x=\lambda/a,y=\lambda/b,z=\lambda/c\).
paragraphs: Set \(F=u+\mu(x^{-1}+y^{-1}+z^{-1}-1)\). Then \(2a^3x-\mu/x^2=0\) and the corresponding y,z equations hold.
Consequently \(2a^3x^3=2b^3y^3=2c^3z^3=\mu\). Taking real cube roots gives \(ax=by=cz=\lambda\).
accordions.final_answer: \(x=(a+b+c)/a,y=(a+b+c)/b,z=(a+b+c)/c\), when these expressions satisfy the stated nonzero-variable constraint.

accordions.title: Example 5.56
question_paragraphs: Find the greatest volume of a rectangular parallelepiped inscribed in \(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2=1\).
paragraphs: Let 2x,2y,2z be the positive full edges, parallel to the ellipsoid’s axes; \(V=8xyz\). Form \(F=8xyz+\lambda(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2-1)\).
The derivative equations, multiplied by x,y,z respectively, imply \(x^2/a^2=y^2/b^2=z^2/c^2\).
The constraint makes each ratio1/3. Hence \(x=a/\sqrt3,y=b/\sqrt3,z=c/\sqrt3\).
The volume is zero on the boundary of the positive feasible octant and positive inside, so this interior stationary volume is the greatest.

accordions.title: Example 5.57
question_paragraphs: Find the stationary values of \(u=x^2/a^4+y^2/b^4+z^2/c^4\), subject to \(lx+my+nz=0\) and \(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2=1\). Interpret the result geometrically.
paragraphs: The x-equation is \(2x/a^4+\lambda_1l+2\lambda_2x/a^2=0\); there are corresponding y,z equations.
Multiply by x,y,z and add. The constraints give \(2u+2\lambda_2=0\), so \(\lambda_2=-u\). Thus

Substitution into the plane relation gives \(l^2a^4/(1-a^2u)+m^2b^4/(1-b^2u)+n^2c^4/(1-c^2u)=0\) in the non-singular case. If a denominator vanishes, check the original multiplier equations before dividing.

PankusDesk completion for singular cases: retain the polynomial form \[l^2a^4(1-b^2u)(1-c^2u)+m^2b^4(1-a^2u)(1-c^2u)+n^2c^4(1-a^2u)(1-b^2u)=0.\] It is the determinant condition for the original multiplier equations together with lx+my+nz=0, and retains the possible roots lost by division. With positive a,b,c and a nonzero plane normal, its two roots (counting multiplicity) are the stationary values on the central ellipse. Recover a nonzero stationary direction from the original linear system and scale it to satisfy the ellipsoid constraint.
The tangent plane to the ellipsoid at \((x,y,z)\) is \(xX/a^2+yY/b^2+zZ/c^2=1\). Its distance p from the origin satisfies \(p^{-2}=x^2/a^4+y^2/b^4+z^2/c^4=u\).

title: Evaluation of Double Integrals in Cartesian coordinates
learn: Integrate from the innermost variable outward; keep other variables fixed.

sections.heading: 7.1 Double integrals
paragraphs: The definite integral is the limit of a sum of values multiplied by lengths. A double integral is its counterpart in two dimensions. Let f(x,y) be defined at every point of a finite region R in the xy-plane. Divide R into elementary areas δA₁,…,δAₙ and choose a point (xᵣ,yᵣ) in each element.

The limit of \(\sum_{r=1}^nf(x_r,y_r)\delta A_r\), if it exists as the number of subdivisions increases indefinitely and every element area tends to zero, is the double integral: \[\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA=\lim\sum_{r=1}^nf(x_r,y_r)\delta A_r.\]

Double integrals are evaluated by successive single integrations. If y₁,y₂ are functions of x and x₁,x₂ are constants, first integrate with respect to y, keeping x fixed; then integrate the resulting expression with respect to x: \[I_1=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\left[\int_{y_1(x)}^{y_2(x)}f(x,y)\,dy\right]dx.\]
Geometrically the inner integral follows a vertical strip from the lower curve to the upper curve. The outer integral slides that strip across the entire region.

If x₁,x₂ are functions of y and y₁,y₂ are constants, first integrate with respect to x, keeping y fixed: \[I_2=\int_{y_1}^{y_2}\left[\int_{x_1(y)}^{x_2(y)}f(x,y)\,dx\right]dy.\] The horizontal strip slides from its lowest to its highest position.
When both pairs of limits are constants, the region is a rectangle. For a continuous integrand on that rectangle either order gives the same value.

sections.heading: 7.3 Double integrals in polar coordinates
paragraphs: To evaluate \(\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)}f(r,\theta)\,dr\,d\theta\), first integrate with respect to r while θ is fixed; then integrate with respect to θ. The limits θ₁,θ₂ are constants.

Geometrically, a radial segment runs from the inner curve r₁ to the outer curve r₂, then turns from the first limiting ray to the second. The order can also be changed if the same region is described with new limits.

title: Evaluation of Triple Integrals
learn: The inner limit may depend on both remaining variables.

sections.heading: 7.5 Triple integrals
paragraphs: Let f(x,y,z) be defined at every point of a finite three-dimensional region V. Divide V into elementary volumes δVᵣ and choose (xᵣ,yᵣ,zᵣ) in each. The limit, if it exists as the subdivisions become indefinitely fine, defines \[\iiint_V f\,dV=\lim\sum_{r=1}^nf(x_r,y_r,z_r)\delta V_r.\]

To evaluate, express the integral as successive integrations. If the x limits are constants, y limits depend on x, and z limits depend on x,y, write \[I=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\int_{y_1(x)}^{y_2(x)}\int_{z_1(x,y)}^{z_2(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.\]
First integrate z with x,y fixed. Next integrate y with x fixed. Finally integrate x. Other orders are possible when the limits are changed to describe the same solid.

title: Change of variables for triple integrals (Cartesian to Spherical coordinates)

sections.heading: 7.7 Change of variables — triple integrals
paragraphs: For a transformation \(x=x(u,v,w)\), \(y=y(u,v,w)\), \(z=z(u,v,w)\), the triple-integral rule is \[\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz=\iiint_{E\prime}f(x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w))|J|\,du\,dv\,dw,\] where \(J=\partial(x,y,z)/\partial(u,v,w)\).

In spherical polar coordinates, r is distance from the origin, θ is the angle from the positive z-axis, and φ is azimuth in the xy-plane: \[x=r\sin\theta\cos\phi,\quad y=r\sin\theta\sin\phi,\quad z=r\cos\theta.\]
The Jacobian is \(r^2\sin\theta\). On the usual ranges r≥0, 0≤θ≤π, 0≤φ<2π, \[dV=r^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi.\]

sections.heading: 7.7 Cylindrical coordinates
paragraphs: For cylindrical coordinates \((\rho,\phi,z)\), \[x=\rho\cos\phi,\qquad y=\rho\sin\phi,\qquad z=z.\] The Jacobian is \[\dfrac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(\rho,\phi,z)}=\rho,\] so \(dV=\rho\,d\rho\,d\phi\,dz\), with the integration order arranged to match the chosen limits.
The radial distance is measured in the xy-plane; z remains the vertical coordinate. A circular cylinder centred on the z-axis becomes a constant radial boundary. A sphere becomes \(\rho^2+z^2=a^2\).

sections.heading: 7.4 Area enclosed by plane curves
paragraphs: For an area bounded by y=f₁(x), y=f₂(x), x=x₁ and x=x₂, divide the region into vertical strips of width δx. Each small rectangle has area δx δy. Summing rectangles along the strip and then summing strips gives \[A=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}\int_{f_1(x)}^{f_2(x)}1\,dy\,dx.\]
For horizontal strips between x=f₁(y) and x=f₂(y), \[A=\int_{y_1}^{y_2}\int_{f_1(y)}^{f_2(y)}1\,dx\,dy.\] Changing the order does not change the area.

In polar coordinates, neighbouring circular arcs and radii form a small curvilinear rectangle. Its radial side is δr and its arc side is r δθ, so its area is approximately r δr δθ. Passing to the limit gives \[A=\iint_R r\,dr\,d\theta.\]
Choose the radial and angular limits to cover the region exactly once. For \(r_1(\theta)\le r\le r_2(\theta)\), \[A=\dfrac12\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\{r_2(\theta)^2-r_1(\theta)^2\}\,d\theta.\]

accordions.title: Example 7.14
question_paragraphs: Find by double integration the area of one quadrant of \(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2=1\), a,b>0.
paragraphs: With vertical strips, \(0\le x\le a\), \(0\le y\le b\sqrt{1-x^2/a^2}\). Hence \[A=\int_0^a\int_0^{b\sqrt{1-x^2/a^2}}dy\,dx=\dfrac ba\int_0^a\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\,dx.\]
Alternatively use horizontal strips: \[A=\int_0^b\int_0^{a\sqrt{1-y^2/b^2}}dx\,dy=\dfrac ab\int_0^b\sqrt{b^2-y^2}\,dy=\dfrac{\pi ab}{4}.\]

sections.heading: 7.6 Volumes of solids
paragraphs: For a nonnegative surface height z=f(x,y) over a plane area S, erect prisms on small rectangles δx δy. Each prism has approximate volume z δx δy. Taking the limit gives \[V=\iint_S f(x,y)\,dx\,dy.\]
In polar coordinates the corresponding expression is \(V=\iint_S z\,r\,dr\,d\theta\).
Alternatively divide a solid into rectangular parallelepipeds with volumes δx δy δz. Their limiting sum is \[V=\iiint_E1\,dx\,dy\,dz,\] with limits covering the solid once.
